question: Under RPL Section 226-c, how much notice is required for a tenant whose occupancy or lease term falls in the middle tier -- more than one year but not more than two years?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 90 days
choice_d: 45 days
explanation: RPL Section 226-c's middle notice tier -- 60 days -- applies to a tenant whose occupancy or lease term is more than one year but not more than two years, falling between the 30-day tier (under one year) and the 90-day tier (over two years).
source_note: RPL Section 226-c (60-day notice tier)

question: A landlord plans to raise a tenant's rent by only 3% at lease renewal. Does RPL Section 226-c require the landlord to give the 30/60/90-day graduated written notice?
choice_a: No -- RPL Section 226-c's graduated notice requirement is only triggered by a rent increase equal to or greater than 5%, or by a decision not to renew
choice_b: Yes, the graduated notice requirement applies to any rent increase of any size
choice_c: No, because RPL Section 226-c never applies to rent increases, only to non-renewals
choice_d: Yes, but only if the tenant has lived there for more than five years
explanation: RPL Section 226-c's graduated 30/60/90-day notice requirement is triggered specifically by a rent increase equal to or greater than 5% above the current rent, or by a landlord's decision not to renew a tenancy -- a smaller increase, such as 3%, does not trigger the statute's notice requirement.
source_note: RPL Section 226-c (5% threshold that triggers the notice requirement)

question: Does RPL Section 226-c's 30/60/90-day notice requirement apply to a rent-stabilized apartment in New York City?
choice_a: RPL Section 226-c governs market-rate residential tenancies statewide; rent-stabilized and rent-controlled units instead follow their own separate renewal and notice framework under the Rent Stabilization Code and Rent Stabilization Law
choice_b: Yes, rent-stabilized tenants receive notice exclusively under RPL Section 226-c and have no other renewal protections
choice_c: No statute of any kind requires notice to rent-stabilized tenants
choice_d: RPL Section 226-c applies only to rent-stabilized units and never to market-rate units
explanation: RPL Section 226-c's graduated notice tiers were enacted to protect market-rate residential tenants statewide who previously had no statutory notice protection; rent-stabilized and rent-controlled tenancies already have their own distinct renewal-notice framework under the Rent Stabilization Code and Rent Stabilization Law, which continues to govern them.
source_note: RPL Section 226-c scope; distinguished from Rent Stabilization Code renewal requirements

question: Before HSTPA's 2019 enactment of RPL Section 227-e, did a New York residential landlord have a legal duty to mitigate damages when a tenant vacated a unit in violation of the lease?
choice_a: No -- prior to RPL Section 227-e, New York followed a 'no mitigation' rule allowing a landlord to leave a unit vacant and sue the departed tenant for the full remaining rent
choice_b: Yes, mitigation had always been mandatory under New York common law
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial leases, never residential
choice_d: The duty to mitigate has existed in New York since the 1970s and predates HSTPA entirely
explanation: Before HSTPA created RPL Section 227-e in 2019, New York followed a long-standing 'no mitigation' rule under which a residential landlord could simply leave a unit vacant after a tenant left in breach of the lease and sue that tenant for the full remaining rent, with no obligation to try to re-rent the unit.
source_note: RPL Section 227-e (2019) -- landlord duty to mitigate damages; prior common-law rule

question: Under RPL Section 227-e, what standard must a landlord meet when attempting to re-rent a unit after a tenant vacates in violation of the lease?
choice_a: In good faith, according to the landlord's resources and abilities, take reasonable and customary actions to re-rent the premises at fair market value or at the rate agreed to during the tenancy, whichever is lower
choice_b: The landlord must hire a licensed broker within 24 hours or forfeit all rights to collect any further rent
choice_c: The landlord has no defined standard to meet -- any effort, however minimal, satisfies the statute
choice_d: The landlord must re-rent at a price at least equal to what the departing tenant was paying, even if that exceeds fair market value
explanation: RPL Section 227-e requires the landlord, in good faith and according to the landlord's resources and abilities, to take reasonable and customary actions to re-rent the premises at fair market value or at the rate agreed to during the tenancy, whichever is lower -- not an unlimited or undefined obligation.
source_note: RPL Section 227-e (mitigation standard)

question: Under RPL Section 227-e, once a landlord successfully re-rents a vacated unit to a new tenant, what is the effect on the departed tenant's liability?
choice_a: The new tenant's lease, once in effect, terminates the departed tenant's lease and mitigates the damages that would otherwise be recoverable against that tenant
choice_b: The departed tenant remains liable for the full original lease term regardless of the new tenancy
choice_c: The new tenant's rent is simply added on top of the departed tenant's remaining obligation
choice_d: The landlord must choose between collecting from the new tenant or the departed tenant, but may never recover a mitigation-reduced amount from both
explanation: Under RPL Section 227-e, once the landlord successfully rents the premises to a new tenant, that new lease terminates the departed tenant's lease and operates to mitigate the damages otherwise recoverable from the tenant who vacated in breach of the lease.
source_note: RPL Section 227-e (effect of re-renting on prior tenant's liability)

question: In a dispute over whether a landlord met the RPL Section 227-e duty to mitigate damages, who bears the burden of proof?
choice_a: The party seeking to recover damages -- typically the landlord -- bears the burden of proving reasonable mitigation efforts were made
choice_b: The departed tenant always bears the burden of proving the landlord failed to mitigate
choice_c: Neither party bears any burden; the court presumes mitigation occurred
choice_d: The burden shifts to the tenant's new landlord at the tenant's next residence
explanation: RPL Section 227-e places the burden of proof on the party seeking to recover damages -- ordinarily the landlord -- meaning the landlord must affirmatively show reasonable and customary re-renting efforts were made before recovering unpaid rent from a tenant who vacated in breach of the lease.
source_note: RPL Section 227-e (burden of proof)

question: Under RPL Section 235-j, New York's bed bug disclosure law, what must a landlord provide to a prospective tenant before they sign a lease?
choice_a: A written disclosure of the one-year bed bug infestation history for both the specific unit and the building as a whole
choice_b: Nothing -- bed bug history is not subject to any mandatory disclosure in New York
choice_c: Only a verbal statement, with no written documentation required
choice_d: A disclosure covering only infestations discovered within the last 30 days
explanation: RPL Section 235-j requires a landlord to provide a new tenant with a written disclosure of the bed bug infestation history for the specific unit being rented and for the building as a whole, covering the preceding one-year period, before the lease is signed.
source_note: RPL Section 235-j (bed bug infestation history disclosure)

question: Under RPL Section 235-j, when a bed bug infestation is discovered in a unit, how quickly must the landlord notify tenants in adjacent, above, and below units, and what may that notice NOT include?
choice_a: Within 72 hours of learning of the infestation, and the notice may not identify the infested unit or include any personally identifying information about the affected tenant
choice_b: Within 30 days, and the notice must name the affected tenant by unit number and name
choice_c: There is no deadline, and the landlord may disclose the tenant's identity freely
choice_d: Within 24 hours, but only if the tenant consents in writing to disclosure
explanation: RPL Section 235-j requires the landlord to notify tenants and lessees in units immediately above, below, or adjacent to an infested unit within 72 hours of learning of the infestation, while prohibiting the notice from identifying the infested unit or including personally identifying information about the affected tenant.
source_note: RPL Section 235-j (72-hour neighbor notification; privacy limitation)

question: Under RPL Section 235-j, may a landlord show or rent a residential unit that the landlord knows currently has an active bed bug infestation?
choice_a: No -- the statute prohibits showing or renting a unit the landlord knows has a current infestation
choice_b: Yes, as long as the rent is discounted to reflect the infestation
choice_c: Yes, without any restriction, so long as pest control has been scheduled
choice_d: Yes, but only if the prospective tenant is informed verbally at the showing
explanation: RPL Section 235-j prohibits a landlord from showing or renting a residential unit that the landlord knows to have a current, active bed bug infestation -- disclosure of past history is not a substitute for this outright prohibition on renting a currently infested unit.
source_note: RPL Section 235-j (prohibition on renting a currently infested unit)

question: Under RPL Section 223-b, what categories of tenant complaints are protected from landlord retaliation?
choice_a: Good faith complaints to the landlord, the landlord's agent, or a government authority regarding health or safety code violations, breach of the warranty of habitability, or the landlord's duty to repair, as well as good faith efforts to enforce lease rights or organize a tenants' union
choice_b: Only complaints filed directly in state Supreme Court
choice_c: Only anonymous complaints submitted through a government hotline
choice_d: No complaints are protected -- New York has no retaliatory eviction statute
explanation: RPL Section 223-b protects a tenant's good faith complaints -- made to the landlord, the landlord's agent, or a governmental authority -- about health or safety violations, breach of the warranty of habitability, or the duty to repair, as well as good faith attempts to enforce lease rights or organize a tenants' union, from landlord retaliation.
source_note: RPL Section 223-b (protected tenant activity)

question: Under RPL Section 223-b, as expanded by HSTPA, within what time period after a tenant's good faith complaint does a landlord's notice to quit, eviction proceeding, or attempt to substantially alter the tenancy create a rebuttable presumption of retaliation?
choice_a: One year -- HSTPA expanded this presumption period from the prior six months
choice_b: Six months, unchanged since before HSTPA
choice_c: 30 days
choice_d: There is no time limit; the presumption applies indefinitely
explanation: HSTPA expanded RPL Section 223-b's retaliation presumption window from six months to one year, so a landlord's notice to quit, eviction proceeding, or attempt to substantially alter the tenancy within one year of a tenant's good faith complaint triggers the rebuttable presumption of retaliation.
source_note: RPL Section 223-b, as expanded by HSTPA (2019) (one-year presumption window)

question: Once a tenant establishes the RPL Section 223-b rebuttable presumption of retaliation, what happens to the burden of proof?
choice_a: The burden shifts to the landlord to establish a non-retaliatory motive for the challenged action by a preponderance of the evidence
choice_b: The case is automatically dismissed with no further proceedings
choice_c: The burden remains entirely on the tenant to disprove the landlord's stated motive
choice_d: The presumption has no legal effect on either party's burden
explanation: Once a tenant establishes the RPL Section 223-b presumption -- for example, by showing the landlord took action within the protected one-year window -- the burden shifts to the landlord to prove a non-retaliatory motive for the action by a preponderance of the evidence.
source_note: RPL Section 223-b (burden-shifting effect of the presumption)

question: What is the basic concept behind New York's Good Cause Eviction Law, effective April 20, 2024?
choice_a: For covered tenancies, a landlord must establish a statutorily defined 'good cause' -- such as nonpayment of rent or lease violation -- to evict a tenant or decline to renew a lease, rather than simply choosing not to renew at will
choice_b: It eliminates all evictions in New York State under any circumstances
choice_c: It applies exclusively to commercial leases and has no residential application
choice_d: It requires every residential tenant to reapply for a new lease each year through a government agency
explanation: New York's Good Cause Eviction Law, effective April 20, 2024, requires that for covered residential tenancies, a landlord must show a statutorily defined 'good cause' -- such as nonpayment, lease violation, or the owner's need to recover the unit -- to evict a tenant or refuse to renew, rather than declining to renew simply because the lease term ended.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024)

question: Under New York's Good Cause Eviction Law, what rent increase amount is presumptively considered 'unreasonable,' potentially giving a covered tenant a defense against eviction?
choice_a: An increase exceeding the lower of 5% plus the regional Consumer Price Index, or 10% annually
choice_b: Any increase exceeding 50% in a single year
choice_c: There is no rent increase threshold anywhere in the law
choice_d: An increase exceeding exactly $500 per month regardless of the base rent
explanation: The Good Cause Eviction Law sets the threshold for a presumptively 'unreasonable' rent increase at the lower of 5% plus the regional Consumer Price Index, or 10% annually -- a covered tenant facing an increase above that threshold may raise a defense in eviction proceedings brought for non-renewal.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) -- rent increase threshold formula

question: Does New York's Good Cause Eviction Law apply automatically statewide, or is its geographic reach more limited?
choice_a: It applies automatically within New York City, while other cities, towns, and villages outside NYC must affirmatively opt in for it to apply locally
choice_b: It applies automatically and uniformly in every municipality across the entire state with no local variation
choice_c: It applies only in rural counties and specifically excludes New York City
choice_d: It has no geographic limitation of any kind and preempts all local housing law
explanation: The Good Cause Eviction Law applies automatically to covered tenancies in New York City, while municipalities outside NYC -- other cities, towns, and villages -- must affirmatively opt in through local legislation before the law applies within their borders.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) -- automatic NYC application vs. opt-in elsewhere

question: Under New York's Good Cause Eviction Law, which landlords qualify for the 'small landlord' exemption?
choice_a: An owner of no more than 10 residential units statewide
choice_b: An owner of no more than 500 residential units statewide
choice_c: Any owner who has held the property for less than one year
choice_d: There is no small landlord exemption anywhere in the law
explanation: The Good Cause Eviction Law exempts a 'small landlord' -- defined as an owner of no more than 10 residential units statewide -- from the law's coverage, on the theory that individual and small-scale owners face different practical constraints than large institutional landlords.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) -- small landlord exemption (10 units)

question: Besides the small landlord exemption, which of the following is also exempt from New York's Good Cause Eviction Law?
choice_a: Units in buildings constructed after 2009, owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 11 units, high-rent units above a defined fair-market-rent multiple, and units already rent-regulated or subsidized
choice_b: Every unit built before 1929, regardless of any other factor
choice_c: Nothing else is exempt -- the small landlord exemption is the law's only carve-out
choice_d: Only units located outside New York State
explanation: In addition to the small landlord exemption, the Good Cause Eviction Law exempts units in buildings first certified for occupancy after 2009, owner-occupied buildings with fewer than 11 units, units renting above a defined high-rent threshold tied to fair market rent, and units that are already rent-stabilized, rent-controlled, or otherwise subsidized.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) -- additional exemptions

question: Before the 2024 Good Cause Eviction Law, could a New York landlord of a free-market (non-regulated), non-covered residential unit simply decline to renew a tenant's lease at the end of its term without stating any reason?
choice_a: Yes -- for a free-market unit outside any regulatory scheme, a landlord could generally decline to renew at lease end without needing to show cause, so long as any required RPL Section 226-c notice was properly given
choice_b: No -- New York has required landlords to show good cause to evict every residential tenant since the 1970s
choice_c: No -- non-renewal without cause has always been illegal statewide for any residential unit
choice_d: Yes, but only if the tenant was more than 90 days delinquent on rent
explanation: Prior to the 2024 Good Cause Eviction Law, a landlord of a free-market, non-regulated residential unit could generally choose not to renew a tenancy at the end of the lease term without stating a reason, provided any applicable RPL Section 226-c notice was timely given -- the Good Cause Eviction Law changed this baseline for covered tenancies by requiring a stated legal justification.
source_note: Good Cause Eviction Law (2024) contrasted with pre-2024 baseline for free-market tenancies

question: Under New York's 'Amanda's Law,' codified at Executive Law Section 378(5-a), what must most residential property owners statewide install?
choice_a: An operable carbon monoxide detector, in one- and two-family homes, condominiums, cooperatives, and multiple dwellings that have a carbon monoxide source
choice_b: A fire sprinkler system in every unit regardless of building size
choice_c: A backup generator sufficient to power the entire building
choice_d: A private security guard stationed at every entrance
explanation: Amanda's Law, codified at Executive Law Section 378(5-a), requires operable carbon monoxide detectors statewide in one- and two-family homes, condominium and cooperative units, and multiple dwellings that have a carbon monoxide source such as fuel-burning equipment or an attached garage.
source_note: Executive Law Section 378(5-a), Amanda's Law (statewide carbon monoxide detector requirement)

question: What is the basic eligibility criterion for a New York City apartment to fall under rent stabilization?
choice_a: Generally, a building of six or more residential units constructed before January 1, 1974, occupied by a tenant who took occupancy after June 30, 1971
choice_b: Any apartment anywhere in New York State built at any time, regardless of unit count
choice_c: Only single-family homes built after 2000
choice_d: Only units owned by the New York City Housing Authority
explanation: Rent stabilization in New York City generally covers buildings of six or more residential units built before January 1, 1974, where the tenant took occupancy after June 30, 1971 -- a NYC-specific regulatory framework distinct from the statewide market-rate protections under RPL Section 226-c.
source_note: NYC Rent Stabilization Law / Emergency Tenant Protection Act eligibility basics (NYC-specific, not statewide)

question: In New York City's rent stabilization system, which body sets the maximum percentage rent increases permitted for stabilized units each year?
choice_a: The New York City Rent Guidelines Board
choice_b: The individual property owner, without any governmental limitation
choice_c: The federal Department of Housing and Urban Development
choice_d: The New York State Attorney General's office
explanation: Under NYC's rent stabilization system, the New York City Rent Guidelines Board annually sets the maximum percentage rent increases landlords may charge for one-year and two-year renewal leases on stabilized units -- a NYC-specific mechanism separate from the statewide RPL Section 226-c notice framework.
source_note: NYC Rent Guidelines Board (NYC-specific rent stabilization mechanism)

question: For a rent-stabilized NYC apartment, within what window before the existing lease expires must the landlord offer the tenant a renewal lease (on DHCR Form RTP-8)?
choice_a: Not more than 150 days and not less than 90 days before the existing lease expires
choice_b: Exactly 30 days before expiration, with no other window permitted
choice_c: Anytime within the last week before the lease expires
choice_d: There is no deadline; the landlord may send the offer at any point, even after expiration
explanation: For a rent-stabilized unit, the owner must offer a written renewal lease, by mail or personal delivery, not more than 150 days and not less than 90 days before the existing lease expires -- a distinct NYC-specific renewal timing rule separate from RPL Section 226-c's 30/60/90-day notice tiers for market-rate units.
source_note: NYC Rent Stabilization Code -- 90-150 day renewal lease offer window (DHCR Form RTP-8)

question: In New York City, what must an owner of a multiple dwelling designate and register with the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)?
choice_a: A managing agent who is in control of and responsible for the building's maintenance and operation and is authorized to address emergency conditions or repairs on the owner's behalf
choice_b: A tenant representative elected annually by building residents
choice_c: A licensed engineer who must reside on-site at all times
choice_d: Nothing -- NYC has no managing agent registration requirement of any kind
explanation: NYC's Multiple Dwelling Registration requirements obligate a building owner to designate and register a managing agent -- who is in control of and responsible for the building's maintenance and operation and authorized to handle emergency conditions or repairs -- with HPD, including a NYC business address for that agent.
source_note: NYC Administrative Code / HPD Multiple Dwelling Registration (managing agent designation, NYC-specific)

question: When a real estate broker takes on rental property management for an owner-client, what should the written property management agreement between them typically define?
choice_a: The scope of the broker's authority, the services to be performed, the compensation structure, and the agreement's term and termination provisions
choice_b: Nothing needs to be defined in writing; an oral understanding is legally sufficient and standard practice
choice_c: Only the broker's compensation, since New York law does not regulate any other term of a property management agreement
choice_d: Only the tenant's obligations, since the owner's and broker's respective duties are implied by default and never need to be stated
explanation: A sound property management agreement between a broker and an owner-client should clearly define the scope of the broker's authority (e.g., leasing, rent collection, maintenance oversight), the specific services to be performed, how and when the broker is compensated, and the term of the agreement along with how either party may terminate it.
source_note: Property management agreement fundamentals (general real estate practice)

question: When a licensed broker acts as a property manager for an owner-client, do the broker's core fiduciary duties (loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care, and accounting) still apply, the same as in a sales transaction?
choice_a: Yes -- a broker acting as a property manager remains an agent of the owner-client and continues to owe the same core fiduciary duties that apply in a sales agency relationship
choice_b: No -- fiduciary duties apply exclusively to sales transactions and have no bearing on property management
choice_c: No -- a property-managing broker owes fiduciary duties only to the tenant, never to the owner
choice_d: Fiduciary duties apply only if the property management agreement expressly states so in writing; otherwise none apply
explanation: A broker who takes on property management for an owner-client remains that owner's agent and continues to owe the same core fiduciary duties recognized in New York agency law -- loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, reasonable care, and accounting -- that apply in a sales agency relationship; the underlying transaction type does not eliminate the fiduciary relationship.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A fiduciary duty principles, applied to property management agency

question: Under GOL Section 7-103, when a residential building has six or more family dwelling units, how must the landlord hold tenants' security deposits?
choice_a: As trust funds, deposited in an interest-bearing account at a New York banking organization, with the landlord entitled to retain up to 1% per annum as an administration expense
choice_b: As the landlord's own general operating funds, with no trust or interest obligation of any kind
choice_c: In cash only, physically stored on the premises
choice_d: In an out-of-state account chosen at the landlord's sole discretion, exempt from New York banking regulation
explanation: GOL Section 7-103 requires that, for buildings with six or more family dwelling units, security deposits be treated as trust funds and deposited in an interest-bearing account at a New York banking organization; the landlord may retain up to 1% per annum of the deposited amount as an administration expense, with the remaining interest belonging to the tenant.
source_note: General Obligations Law Section 7-103 (interest-bearing trust account requirement, buildings with 6+ units)
